I have been working this land for 55 years. I know what grows here, what the soil wants, and what my body can still manage at 73. My legs are not what they were, so I think carefully about what is worth the labor. My children send some money back from the city, but I still need this farm to pull its weight.

Quzhou has always been cotton country. Cotton is what I know best, and the soil on my better plots suits it. I will put 2 mu into cotton — my main effort. The other fields I rotate wheat in winter, then maize in summer on the same 1.5 mu of ground. That system has worked for decades and I see no reason to change it. Stevia is new for me — only started a few years back — but the collection company comes to the village and the price is fair for what little work it takes. I keep 0.6 mu in stevia.

For seed, I use what the township extension station recommends for wheat — improved varieties outyield the old ones. Maize I have used hybrid seed for years now, same as all my neighbors. For cotton I stay with improved but not hybrid — hybrid cotton needs more precise management and my eyes are not sharp enough for that anymore. Stevia I get from the same supplier as before.

Water I manage carefully because the pump electricity adds up. Cotton I water four times — emergence, flowering, boll set, and one more if the summer is dry. Wheat gets three irrigations — winter freeze protection, green-up in spring, and before heading. Maize only needs two because it mostly rains in July and August. Stevia needs water but is forgiving.

Pesticides: cotton always needs the most attention. Aphids every year, spider mites in the hot dry spells, bollworm some years. I spray five times, roughly every two weeks from June through August. Wheat gets two sprays — one for powdery mildew, one for aphids at heading. Maize and stevia I spray lightly, two or three times each.

Fertilizer: I apply base fertilizer by plough before planting, then top-dress during the season. My amounts reflect what I have learned yields well without wasting money on excess.
